content: The procurement of medicines is typically managed at a higher administrative level. However, if rifampicin is procured at a peripheral level, it must adhere to the established policies. It is essential to inform them that single-dose rifampicin (SDR-PEP) significantly reduces the risk of developing leprosy. Local advocacy and information, education, and communication (IEC) activities should be conducted periodically if contact tracing or PEP is implemented year-round, or a few weeks before the start of a campaign if the activities are conducted in a campaign format. Any additional activities should be decided at the local level. The annual leprosy plan at the district or community level should include all necessary activities for implementing contact tracing and/or PEP. These activities include local advocacy, training or orientation of staff and volunteers, procurement and distribution of rifampicin (preferably alongside multidrug therapy drugs), establishing a referral system, planning contact tracing, and ensuring monitoring and supervision. Ideally, contact tracing and PEP should be integrated into the regular leprosy control or broader health plans for the district, rather than creating a separate plan. This integration allows for monitoring the overall progress of contact tracing and PEP as part of leprosy control activities. Monitoring and supervision are essential tools for program management, designed to track the progress of planned activities and assess the program's performance. Monitoring involves the continuous flow of information within the program chain, supported by periodic or ad-hoc progress reports. It relies on specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART) objectives and indicators that are easy to collect. Supervision, on the other hand, focuses on ensuring and improving the quality of services, particularly by assessing and enhancing staff performance. Supportive supervision fosters improvement through collaboration, setting uniform standards, identifying and solving problems, addressing needs, and providing development opportunities. More details on monitoring and supervision can be found in the WHO Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020 Monitoring and Evaluation Guide. Monitoring and supervision related to contact tracing and PEP can be integrated into the overall assessment of leprosy programs or community outreach activities across public health interventions. Monitoring the implementation of planned activities and supervising the performance of health staff and community health volunteers can be achieved by accompanying them during their work, using checklists, and making observations. Checklists can be used for various aspects of the program, such as: Enrollment of index cases: Ensuring that identified index cases match the treatment register and that all index cases have been counseled on leprosy basics and the benefits of contact tracing and PEP. Contact listing and tracing: Verifying that the index case has consented to disclose their disease status for contact tracing. The contact list should be as complete as possible, with accurate details recorded. Visits to listed contacts should be confirmed, and counseling on disease transmission and prevention should be cross-checked. Contact screening: Ensuring that contacts understand the importance of screening and have provided consent for physical examinations. Supervisors can observe screenings or interview contacts to confirm proper procedures were followed. PEP administration: Ensuring contacts are adequately counseled about the benefits and limitations of SDR-PEP, including its limited efficacy and potential side effects. Evidence should confirm that exclusion and inclusion criteria were checked before administering SDR. Supervisors should address refusals by convincing contacts of the benefits of PEP. Drug management: Ensuring adequate availability of rifampicin in various dosages, timely procurement, proper storage according to guidelines, and adherence to the first expiry, first out principle. Expiry dates should be checked regularly. Record and report monitoring: Ensuring that patient treatment cards, contact lists, and drug registers are complete and properly maintained. Reports should be compiled accurately, submitted on time, and any feedback received should be acted upon. Indicators can be used to assess the implementation of contact screening and/or PEP. These indicators include the number of index cases enrolled, the number of contacts listed, the average number of contacts per index case, the number of contacts screened, the proportion of contacts screened, the number of contacts receiving SDR, and the proportion of contacts receiving SDR. Additionally, the number of leprosy cases detected among contacts and the proportion of cases detected through contact tracing can be calculated. These indicators can be collected monthly, quarterly, or annually and aggregated at higher levels for analysis. Information, education, and communication (IEC) are critical components of public health programs. An informed community fosters demand for services, and well-informed patients are more likely to comply with treatment. Simple messages such as Leprosy can now be prevented or A single dose of rifampicin can significantly reduce the risk of developing leprosy should be communicated in a language understood by the target audience, avoiding medical jargon. These messages provide hope to patients, their families, and the community. Consent forms for index cases and contacts should clearly explain the nature of leprosy, its transmission, and the benefits of screening and PEP. Index cases must agree to disclose their disease status to facilitate contact tracing, while contacts must consent to screening and the administration of rifampicin. Both forms should emphasize the safety and efficacy of rifampicin in preventing leprosy and outline the steps to take in case of adverse effects.
